diagrams.title: Types of oral health examination (ADA Types I–IV)

cloze.section: Role of the dental hygienist in public health
cloze.text: In public health, the dental hygienist as {{c1::advocate}} promotes changes through legislation and policy.

cloze.section: Role of the dental hygienist in public health
cloze.text: In public health, the dental hygienist as {{c1::researcher}} collects data and communicates scientific findings.

cloze.section: Role of the dental hygienist in public health
cloze.text: In public health, the dental hygienist as {{c1::administrator}} manages, develops and coordinates oral health programs.

cloze.section: Role of the dental hygienist in public health
cloze.text: In public health, the dental hygienist as {{c1::clinician}} provides patient care; as {{c2::educator}} she educates students and the community.
{{c1::Primary}} prevention examples: oral prophylaxis, community water fluoridation, athletic mouthguards, pit and fissure sealants, nutrition education.
{{c1::Secondary}} prevention examples: oral cancer screening, tobacco cessation, drilling and filling a cavity, periodontal therapy, silver diamine fluoride for caries.
cloze.extra: The book also lists periodontal therapy under tertiary prevention in its bullet list; its summary table puts it under secondary.

cloze.text: {{c1::Tertiary}} prevention examples: replacing missing teeth (dentures, implants, bridges), bone and tissue grafts.
Dental caries is the {{c1::most common chronic childhood disease}} — about {{c2::five}} times more common than asthma — and a major reason children miss school days.
Low {{c1::socioeconomic status}} is strongly related to caries risk.
Root caries risk increases with age because of {{c1::gingival recession}}, {{c2::medications causing xerostomia}}, and lack of oral care.
Caries prevention through dietary education: e.g., helping school children differentiate {{c1::cariogenic}} food from less cariogenic food.
cloze.extra: Other caries-prevention measures in the book: sealants, fluoride therapy (e.g., fluoride varnish to create stronger teeth), oral hygiene education (e.g., brushing techniques).

cloze.text: Periodontal diseases affect approximately {{c1::half}} of the U.S. population; about {{c2::70%}} of patients 65 and older have periodontitis.
{{c1::Bacteria}} are the primary cause of periodontal disease.
{{c1::Smoking}} is one of the most important risk factors for periodontal disease.
Other periodontal disease risk factors: gender ({{c1::men}}), {{c2::rural}} living, low socioeconomic status and low education level.
The major risk factors for oral cancer are {{c1::smoking}} and {{c1::alcohol}} consumption.
5A tobacco-cessation model: {{c1::Ask}} about tobacco use at every visit; {{c2::Advise}} all tobacco users to quit.
5A tobacco-cessation model: {{c1::Assess}} willingness to quit; {{c2::Assist}} the patient in quitting; {{c3::Arrange}} follow-up contact.
Tobacco education should start at a {{c1::young}} age: nearly {{c2::90%}} of adults who smoke daily had their first cigarette by age {{c3::18}} (CDC).
Teach patients {{c1::self-examination}} of the oral cavity to detect abnormalities such as pigmentation.
{{c1::Systemic}} fluoride is swallowed, circulates through the body, and becomes part of the developing tooth structure {{c2::before the teeth erupt}}.
{{c1::Topical}} fluoride is applied directly to the tooth surface after the teeth have erupted; it strengthens enamel and helps {{c2::reverse early decay}}.

Community water fluoridation is the single {{c1::most effective}} public health measure to prevent tooth decay; the CDC named it one of the {{c2::10}} greatest public health achievements of the 20th century.
Community water fluoridation is very inexpensive: {{c1::$0.12 to $1.16}} per individual per year; a lifetime of fluoridated water costs less than {{c2::one dental filling}}.
If a patient's teeth show {{c1::fluorosis}}, check the fluoride level in the drinking water — fluoride levels in {{c2::well water}} vary.
Bottled water usually contains less than {{c1::0.3}} ppm fluoride; FDA regulations require listing fluoride only if it is {{c2::added during processing}}.
School water fluoridation adds fluoride to the drinking water supply at schools; it is useful in areas where {{c1::community water fluoridation is not available}}.
In school water fluoridation the fluoride concentration is {{c1::4–5 times}} higher than community water levels because children are at school only part of each day and year.
School water fluoridation: children should start in {{c1::earlier}} grades for maximum effect, and administrators require {{c2::parents' consent}}.

A school fluoride rinse program is a supervised program in which children {{c1::rinse their mouths with a fluoride solution}}; it is useful where community water fluoridation is not available but is no longer widely used because it is not {{c2::cost-effective}}.
School fluoride rinse: concentration {{c1::0.2%}}; rinse for {{c2::60 seconds}} once a {{c3::week}}.
In a school fluoride rinse program, {{c1::non-dental personnel}} (e.g., a teacher) can provide the rinse; administrators require parents' consent.
The age at which fluoride toothpaste should be used may vary according to the patient's {{c1::socioeconomic status}} or {{c1::caries risk}}.
Fluoride toothpaste amount: younger than 3 years — a {{c1::smear layer (rice-sized)}} amount; 3–6 years — a {{c2::pea-size}} amount.

Fluoride varnish is well tolerated (children and seniors), easy to apply and needs no special equipment; apply every {{c1::3}} months for high caries risk and every {{c2::6}} months for moderate caries risk.
Fluoride varnish is {{c1::5% sodium fluoride (NaF)}}, {{c2::22,600}} ppm; it is the {{c3::most common}} professional fluoride today — adheres to teeth with minimal ingestion.
cloze.extra: Typical use: high caries risk (children & seniors); easy application in clinics/schools.

cloze.text: Professional fluoride gel or foam in trays: {{c1::1.23% acidulated phosphate fluoride (APF)}}, {{c2::12,300}} ppm.
Avoid APF fluoride in patients with {{c1::porcelain, composites or sealants}} because it may {{c2::etch}} these surfaces.
Professional {{c1::2% NaF}} gel ({{c2::9,050}} ppm) is applied in trays or brushed on; a {{c3::4}}-minute tray application, safe for restorations.
OTC toothpaste (NaF, SnF<sub>2</sub>, etc.) contains {{c1::1,000–1,500}} ppm fluoride; for daily home use by all age groups — {{c2::supervising young children}} is critical.
Prescription toothpaste is {{c1::5,000}} ppm NaF, for adults with {{c2::high caries risk or xerostomia}}; used daily instead of OTC toothpaste.
OTC fluoride rinse (NaF or SnF<sub>2</sub>) contains {{c1::200–1,000}} ppm; for moderate-risk patients, {{c2::orthodontic appliances}}, early demineralization; typically used once or twice daily.
cloze.extra: Not for children under 6 (risk of swallowing).

cloze.text: Prescription fluoride rinse is {{c1::900}} ppm ({{c2::0.2%}}) NaF, for high-risk patients.
Daily dietary fluoride supplements (drops or tablets) are given to children from {{c1::6 months}} to {{c2::16 years}} of age, in areas {{c3::without fluoridated water}}.
The dose of a fluoride supplement depends on the child's {{c1::age}} and the {{c2::fluoride level already in the drinking water}}.
The risk of {{c1::dental fluorosis}} increases if fluoride supplements are taken above recommended amounts.
No fluoride supplement is given from birth to {{c1::6 months}}, or at any age when the drinking water contains more than {{c2::0.6}} ppm fluoride.
Community programs parallel private practice: needs assessment/survey ↔ {{c1::assessment/examination}}; analysis/prioritization of needs ↔ {{c2::diagnosis}}; financing ↔ {{c3::payment}}.
cloze.extra: Program planning ↔ treatment planning; program implementation ↔ treatment implementation; evaluation ↔ evaluation.

cloze.text: Community assessment establishes a {{c1::baseline}}, {{c2::quantifies}} the issue, defines scope/severity and root cause, and creates a community profile.

Assessment data: {{c1::population characteristics}} (race, geographic distribution, education, income), {{c2::resources}} (facilities, funding, policies, labor) and {{c3::oral diseases}} (rate of tooth decay, oral cancer).
Assessment method: the {{c1::interview}} is time-consuming and not adequate for large groups.
cloze.extra: Other assessment methods: questionnaires, reviewing existing documents.

cloze.text: Assessment method: {{c1::direct observation}} is the best method for detailed assessment and is unbiased by the subject, but is time-consuming and not cost-effective for large groups.
Type I ({{c1::complete}}) examination: mouth mirror, explorer, light, radiographs, study models and tests; {{c2::seldom}} used in a public health setting.
Type II (limited) examination: mouth mirror, explorer, light, {{c1::bitewings and selected periapicals}}.
Type III ({{c1::inspection}}) examination: mouth mirror, explorer and light only; the {{c2::most used}} method in public health surveys.
Type IV (screening) examination: light and {{c1::tongue depressor}} only; too {{c2::unreliable}} for public health surveys.
{{c1::Barriers to care}} are anything that limits the ability to receive dental services, e.g., age, language, lack of transportation, lack of a dental provider, attitudes, beliefs.
Program analysis is also called {{c1::prioritization of needs}}: determining which oral health problems are most important and where to focus limited resources.
{{c1::Normative}} need tells what people clinically need, based on exams or professional judgment (e.g., how many people need a filling or periodontal treatment).
{{c1::Use}} shows what services people are receiving over a certain time (e.g., the percentage of children who received fluoride varnish in the past year).
{{c1::Demand}} reflects how many people need care AND are actively seeking it — perceived need turning into demand (e.g., parents requesting sealants for their children).
Program planning includes setting {{c1::goals}} and {{c1::objectives}}, finding resources and organizing logistics.

A {{c1::goal}} describes the major purpose of the plan (e.g., improve oral home care of children at Orange Elementary School); an {{c2::objective}} describes specific details to achieve it (e.g., children will demonstrate circular brushing technique by the end of the program).
Objectives should be specific (provide {{c1::details}}), measurable ({{c2::outcomes}} can be compared) and time-limited (an {{c3::endpoint}} is stated).
{{c1::Implementation}} is the action phase of a program, where everything planned is put into motion.
{{c1::Formal}} delivery is structured and instructor-led (lectures, group discussions, dental services); {{c2::informal}} delivery is passive or self-directed (videos, pamphlets, posters).
Program evaluation measures success by reviewing whether the {{c1::goals/objectives}} were achieved and what {{c2::impact}} the program had on the target population.
Formal evaluation methods (tests, surveys, clinical exams) are {{c1::quantitative}}; informal methods (feedback, interviews, observations) are {{c2::qualitative}}.

Patient-using theories are theoretical models or frameworks that explain how patients {{c1::engage with and manage their health care}}; dental hygiene uses them to guide patient-centered care, motivation and {{c2::behavior change}}.
Learning ladder — {{c1::unawareness}}: the patient lacks information or has incorrect information (e.g., believes brushing once a day is enough).
cloze.extra: Mnemonic (top → bottom): Hippos Are Into Snacks And Umbrellas.

cloze.text: Learning ladder — {{c1::awareness}}: the patient knows a problem exists but hasn't taken any action yet (e.g., hears flossing prevents gum disease but doesn't think it applies to them).
Learning ladder — {{c1::self-interest}}: the patient understands the issue and begins to show personal interest in making a change (e.g., notices bleeding and asks if flossing will help).
Learning ladder — {{c1::involvement}}: the patient wants more information and is willing to act (e.g., asks about the cost of water flossing devices).
Learning ladder — {{c1::action}}: the patient takes steps to solve the problem (e.g., begins to use the water flosser once a week).
Learning ladder — {{c1::habit}}: the behavior becomes part of the patient's lifestyle and the change is sustained (e.g., uses a water flosser daily at home).

The Health Belief Model explains how a patient's {{c1::beliefs}} influence their behavior; it helps dental professionals understand and {{c2::predict}} whether a patient will take action to improve oral health.
Learning domains describe different ways people learn, helping dental professionals {{c1::tailor education}} to the patient's needs.
Locus of control is how much control a person {{c1::feels}} they have over their health and decisions.
Maslow's hierarchy of needs: people must meet {{c1::basic needs}} before they can focus on {{c2::higher-level goals}} like learning and behavior change.

basic.back: Preventing disease before it even starts
Early detection and prompt intervention, before significant damage occurs

basic.front: A dental hygienist starts a school fluoride varnish program because she has observed dental caries in the group. Which level of prevention is this?
basic.back: Secondary prevention (responding to disease already observed)
basic.extra: If she uses the same program to PREVENT caries (none observed yet), it is primary prevention.

basic.front: Do prenatal fluoride supplements (taken by the mother during pregnancy) benefit the unborn child?
basic.back: No — there is no proven benefit.
Evaluation done DURING a program to make improvements along the way (e.g., a weekly survey)
Evaluation done AFTER a program to assess its overall success (e.g., a final survey)
Learning domain of knowledge and intellectual skills
basic.extra: e.g., a clinician gives a brochure explaining different brushing techniques for the patient to review.

basic.back: Learning domain of attitudes, values and feelings toward a topic
basic.extra: e.g., a teacher discusses the benefits of fluoride with parents to shape their attitudes and support.

basic.back: Learning domain of physical movement and use of motor skills
basic.extra: e.g., a hygienist demonstrates proper brushing and the patient practices in front of her.

basic.back: The patient believes they have personal control over their health
basic.extra: e.g., "If I floss every day, I can avoid gum disease."

basic.back: The patient believes their health is controlled by external forces like fate, luck or genetics
basic.extra: e.g., "No matter what I do, I always get cavities; I have bad genes."

typein.question: Sealants give the best results when applied within how many months of molar eruption? (number)
1 ppm of fluoride equals how many mg/L? (number)
typein.extra: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L = 1 drop (0.05 mL) of fluoride in 50 liters of water (about a large bathtub).

typein.question: What is the recommended fluoride level for community water? (ppm, number)
Water containing more than how many ppm of fluoride undergoes defluoridation? (number)
A fluoride rinse is not advised for children under what age? (years, number)
typein.extra: Or until the child can properly spit.

typein.question: Fluoride supplement: child 6 months–3 years, drinking water <0.3 ppm. Daily dose? (mg/day, number)
Fluoride supplement: child 3–6 years, drinking water <0.3 ppm. Daily dose? (mg/day, number)
Fluoride supplement: child 3–6 years, drinking water 0.3–0.6 ppm. Daily dose? (mg/day, number)
Fluoride supplement: child 6–16 years, drinking water <0.3 ppm. Daily dose? (mg/day, number)
Fluoride supplement: child 6–16 years, drinking water 0.3–0.6 ppm. Daily dose? (mg/day, number)
How many mg of sodium fluoride contain 1 mg of fluoride ion? (number)
How many stages does the learning ladder have? (number)
typein.extra: The stages a person goes through when adopting a new health behavior; helps the clinician assess where the patient stands.

mcq.question: A community clinic replaces missing teeth with partial dentures for low-income seniors. This is an example of which level of prevention?
mcq.explanation: Tertiary prevention restores function and rehabilitates after disease has caused damage (dentures, implants, bridges, grafts). Secondary prevention would be early detection/intervention, such as an oral cancer screening or filling a cavity.

mcq.question: A patient who smokes 10 cigarettes a day says he knows he should stop but is not sure he wants to try yet. Following the 5A model, the hygienist has just asked and advised. What is the NEXT step?
options: B. Assess his willingness to quit
C. Assist him with a quit plan
D. Ask about tobacco use again
mcq.answer: B. Assess his willingness to quit
mcq.explanation: The 5As run Ask → Advise → Assess → Assist → Arrange. After advising, the clinician assesses willingness to quit; assisting comes only after that, and arranging follow-up is last.

mcq.question: Which statement about community water fluoridation is correct?
options: A. The recommended level is 1.2 ppm
B. It costs more per person than a single dental filling over a lifetime
C. The recommended level is 0.7 ppm
D. Bottled water must always list its fluoride content
mcq.answer: C. The recommended level is 0.7 ppm
mcq.explanation: The current recommendation is 0.7 ppm (previously 0.7–1.2). A lifetime of fluoridated water costs LESS than one filling, and the FDA requires fluoride listing on bottled water only if fluoride was added during processing.

mcq.question: A high-caries-risk patient has several porcelain veneers and composite restorations. Which professional fluoride should the hygienist AVOID?
mcq.explanation: Acidulated phosphate fluoride (APF) may etch porcelain, composites and sealants. Neutral sodium fluoride products (varnish, 2% NaF gel) are safe for restorations.

mcq.question: A dental hygienist is planning an oral health survey of 2,000 schoolchildren. Which type of examination is most commonly used for this purpose?
mcq.explanation: Type III (inspection: mirror, explorer, light) is the most used method in public health surveys. Type IV screening (light + tongue depressor) is too unreliable for surveys; Type I needs radiographs and study models and is seldom used in public health.

mcq.question: Parents at an elementary school sign a petition asking the district to provide dental sealants for their children. This best illustrates which concept?
mcq.explanation: Demand = people who need care and actively seek it (perceived need turning into demand). Normative need is defined by professionals from exams; use is the services actually received over a time period.

mcq.question: "By the end of the 6-week program, 80% of third graders will demonstrate the circular brushing technique." This statement is best described as a(n):
mcq.explanation: It is an objective: specific, measurable (80%) and time-limited (6 weeks). A goal states the broad major purpose, e.g., 'improve oral home care of third graders'.

mcq.question: Halfway through a school brushing program, the hygienist surveys teachers each week and adjusts her lessons based on their comments. This is an example of:
mcq.explanation: Formative evaluation happens during the program to make improvements along the way. Summative evaluation happens after the program to judge overall success.

mcq.question: After learning her gums bleed, a patient asks the hygienist which interdental brushes are best and how much they cost. On the learning ladder she is at which stage?
mcq.explanation: Involvement = the patient wants more information and is willing to act (e.g., asking about cost of devices). Self-interest is the earlier step of first showing personal interest; action means she has actually started using the aid.

mcq.question: A patient began flossing daily only after her sister was diagnosed with severe periodontitis. In the Health Belief Model, the sister's diagnosis served as a:
mcq.explanation: A cue to action is a trigger or reminder that prompts the person to act (pain, dentist's advice, a health campaign, an event). Perceived severity is the belief that the consequences are serious — not the trigger itself.

mcq.question: A hygienist hands a patient a power toothbrush, demonstrates the technique, then watches the patient practice it in the chair. Which learning domain is being addressed?
mcq.explanation: Psychomotor = physical movement and motor skills (demonstrate, then practice). Cognitive would be knowledge only, e.g., a brochure explaining techniques.
